france24fr.description: Après plus de deux mois passés à empêcher les navires de rejoindre ou de quitter les ports iraniens, l'armée américaine a annoncé jeudi avoir levé son blocus maritime. Le commandement militaire américain a toutefois prévenu que des bâtiments militaires américains resteraient "dans cette zone pour s'assurer que l'ensemble des aspects de l'accord sont bien respectés et appliqués".

france24fr.title: Vacances plus longues, école plus tôt… Face aux fortes chaleurs, faut-il adapter les rythmes scolaires ?
france24fr.description: Face à la vague de chaleur qui touche la France, plusieurs établissements scolaires ont annoncé modifier leurs horaires dès ce jeudi. Alors que les épisodes comme celui-ci sont voués à se multiplier sous l'effet du dérèglement climatique, le débat est relancé : faut-il aménager les rythmes scolaires en fonction du mercure ? Une question déjà omniprésente dans les pays du Sud depuis plusieurs années.

france24fr.title: L'Iran a-t-il fait plier Trump ?
france24fr.description: Le protocole d'accord signé entre les États-Unis et l'Iran ouvre aujourd'hui une période de négociations de 60 jours en vue d'un accord définitif. L'Iran s'engage à ne pas développer ni acquérir l'arme nucléaire, tandis que Washington prévoit de lever l'ensemble des sanctions en cas d'accord définitif. Le détroit d'Ormuz doit être rouvert rapidement et le blocus américain levé dans les 30 jours. Selon JD Vance, le compte à rebours des négociations commence aujourd'hui.

france24fr.title: Mondial 2026 : Tchèques et Sud-Africains se neutralisent, un nul qui n'arrange personne
france24fr.description: La République tchèque et l'Afrique du Sud ont lancé jeudi la deuxième journée de phase de groupes du Mondial 2026 au Mercedes-Benz Stadium d'Atlanta. La rencontre s'est conclue par un match nul (1-1) qui n'arrange personne en vue de la qualification pour les 16es de finale. Les Tchèques ont voulu gérer leur avance, mais les Sud-Africains ont recollé sur penalty en fin de match.

france24fr.title: Accord entre l'Iran et les États-Unis : une victoire pour Téhéran ?
france24fr.description: Un protocole d’accord en 14 points a été signé à Versailles entre les États-Unis et l’Iran, ouvrant une période de négociations de 60 jours. Si Donald Trump se rengorge de cette signature, certains y voient surtout une victoire pour Téhéran. Roselyne Febvre reçoit Jacques Audibert, ancien conseiller diplomatique de François Hollande, Catherine Tricot, directrice de la revue Regards, et Éric Le Boucher, éditorialiste aux Échos et à L’Opinion.

france24fr.title: Moscou : une importante raffinerie touchée par une attaque ukrainienne
france24fr.description: Une importante raffinerie moscovite a été touchée ce jeudi 18 juin par la plus importante attaque de drones de l'Ukraine contre Moscou depuis au moins deux ans.

france24fr.title: Mondial 2026 : Maroc, Cap-Vert, Tunisie… Le carnet de notes des équipes africaines
france24fr.description: La première journée a offert quelques bonnes surprises aux dix sélections africaines engagées dans ce Mondial 2026 à 48 équipes. La rédaction de France 24 vous propose de passer en revue l'entrée en lice de ces équipes avant le début de la deuxième journée des phases de poules.

france24fr.title: Attaque de drones sur Moscou : une raffinerie de la capitale russe touchée
france24fr.description: L'Ukraine a lancé tôt jeudi matin sa plus importante attaque de drones contre Moscou depuis au moins deux ans, provoquant des incendies dans la région autour de la capitale russe et perturbant le fonctionnement de ses principaux aéroports, selon les autorités.

france24fr.title: "Je suis honnête" affirme J.-L. Zapatero accusé de trafic d'influence
france24fr.description: Maude Petit-Jové, notre correspondante à Madrid, analyse la situation.

france24fr.title: Travail matinal et rythmes de vie modifiés, comment s'adapter aux canicules ?
france24fr.description: La canicule s'est installée jeudi sur une large partie de la France, de Paris au centre-est, et s'étendra vendredi, avec une cinquantaine de départements en vigilance orange, et plusieurs municipalités annulant la populaire Fête de la musique prévue dimanche.

france24fr.title: Bombardements de Moscou : quand l'Ukraine veut priver la Russie de son or noir
france24fr.description: L’attaque massive de drones menée par l'armée ukrainienne contre la capitale russe visait tout particulièrement la raffinerie de Moscou et s’inscrit dans une campagne intense de bombardements des infrastructures pétrolières russes. Un levier de plus en plus coûteux pour le Kremlin, qui vise à saper sa capacité à financer son effort de guerre.

spiegel.title: Bayreuter Festspiele: Katharina Wagner entschuldigt sich offenbar bei Michel Friedman
spiegel.description: Wegen angeblicher Sicherheitsbedenken wurde eine Veranstaltung über Antisemitismus in Bayreuth abgesagt. Der Autor Michel Friedman sollte dort reden – und zeigte sich empört. Nun rudert Festspiel-Chefin Katharina Wagner laut einem Medienbericht zurück.

spiegel.title: Iran-Deal: JD Vance verbittet sich Kritik aus Israel an Donald Trump
spiegel.description: Im Irankrieg standen Israel und die USA eng zusammen. Nach kritischen Berichten warnt US-Vizepräsident Vance nun jedoch den Partner, nicht den einzigen mächtigen Verbündeten anzugreifen, den man weltweit noch habe.

spiegel.title: Südafrika: Deutscher in Kapstadt vermisst – Geständnis von Überfall
spiegel.description: Nick Frischke kehrte 2023 von einer Wanderung im Umland von Kapstadt nicht zurück, vier Männer werden verdächtigt, den jungen Deutschen überfallen und beraubt zu haben. Nun gibt es neue Hinweise zur Tat.

spiegel.title: NBA: New York Knicks sollen als erste Champions Donald Trump im Weißen Haus besuchen
spiegel.description: Weil der Besitzer der New York Knicks ein Kumpel des US-Präsidenten ist, will er seine Meistermannschaft ins Weiße Haus bringen. Ob die Basketballer überhaupt mitmachen, ist aber noch unklar.

spiegel.title: Omid Nouripour zum Iran-Krieg: »Die Amerikaner haben bedingungslos kapituliert«

spiegel.description: Bereits während ihrer Amtszeiten pflegten Angela Merkel und Barack Obama ein freundschaftliches Verhältnis, nun hat die Altkanzlerin dessen Presidential Center besucht. Merkel ist selbst Teil der Ausstellung in dem Museum.

spiegel.description: Ärztin Cosima Vieth behandelt in der »Praxis ohne Grenzen« nichtversicherte Menschen. Nun steht die Finanzierung auf der Kippe, Vieth appelliert an die Hamburger Regierung. Ein Besuch bei einer Frau, die nicht aufgibt.

spiegel.title: Uno: Kürzt Deutschland nach Abstimmungsdesaster doch seine Beiträge?
spiegel.description: Deutschland ist bei der Wahl im Uno-Sicherheitsrat krachend gescheitert. Zunächst schloss CDU-Außenminister Wadephul aus, deshalb künftig weniger zahlen zu wollen. Jetzt klingt er anders – und eckt damit beim Koalitionspartner an.

spiegel.title: Martin Sellner in Chemnitz: Sparkasse muss kein Konto für »Institut für Remigration« eröffnen
spiegel.description: Die Sparkasse Chemnitz verweigert dem Rechtsextremisten Martin Sellner ein Konto. Dagegen zog der Österreicher vor Gericht und scheiterte mit einem Eilverfahren. Damit will er sich nicht abfinden.

spiegel.title: Nordschwarzwald – Rottweil: Jugendtrainer wegen sexuellen Kindesmissbrauchs angeklagt

spiegel.title: Peine bei Celle: Geflohener Mörder in italienischem Krankenhaus festgenommen
spiegel.description: Der Fall der getöteten Melanie aus Peine sorgte Anfang der Zehnerjahre für Entsetzen. Am Dienstag entkam ihr Mörder bei einem Freigang, seine Flucht endet nun in Italien.

spiegel.title: Fabian aus Güstrow: Zeugin beschreibt inszenierten Leichenfund und Kälte der Angeklagten
spiegel.description: Gina H. soll den achtjährigen Fabian ermordet haben. Eine frühere Freundin sagte nun vor Gericht aus. Sie berichtet von einem inszenierten Leichenfund und einer menschlichen Kälte, die erschüttert.

spiegel.title: »Strangers: A Memoir of Marriage«: Warum so viele Frauen dieses Scheidungsbuch feiern
spiegel.description: Oprah Winfrey nennt es ein Muss, Netflix sicherte sich die Rechte, die Hauptrolle ist bereits starbesetzt: Belle Burdens Memoiren sind ein Phänomen. Dennoch sehen sich Frauen gezwungen, die Autorin zu verteidigen.

spiegel.title: News des Tages: Brandmauer, Drohnenangriff auf Moskau, Hitze in Deutschland
spiegel.description: Nach einem Tabubruch im EU-Parlament kocht die Brandmauer-Debatte wieder hoch. Die Ukraine feiert einen dreifach wichtigen Militärschlag. Und im Spaßbad lauert eine unterschätzte Gefahr. Das ist die Lage am Donnerstagabend.

spiegel.title: Evonik streicht mehr als 2000 Stellen in Deutschland
spiegel.description: Der Chemiekonzern Evonik steckt seit Jahren tief in der Krise. Nun sollen in Deutschland und international erneut Tausende Jobs wegfallen, wenn auch ohne betriebsbedingte Kündigungen.

spiegel.title: Kommentar zum Beschluss der Rückführungsrichtlinie im Europaparlament
spiegel.description: Rechtsextremisten skandieren im Europaparlament, nachdem die sogenannte Rückführungsrichtlinie beschlossen wurde. Das zeigt, auf welchem Irrweg die Politik der Union unterwegs ist.

observador.description: São esperados Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner, negociadores norte-americanos. O Kremlin não adianta datas, mas diz que será brevemente, uma vez que o memorando entre EUA e Irão está assinado.

observador.description: Ana Paula Martins assegura que o plano para o verão está em marcha. Ainda, o líder supremo do Irão avisa que não aceita eventual acordo se os EUA forem muito exigentes.

observador.description: Os dois homens, de 32 e 46 anos e alvo de mandados de captura internacional, foram detidos esta quinta-feira entre as 12h e as 14h20, um em Montemor-o-Velho e o outro em Ansião.

new-sci.title: Remarkable fossils rewrite the story of how animals conquered the land

new-sci.description: An extremely unusual tectonic movement took place 15 minutes after the Tohoku earthquake in 2011, causing almost the whole of Japan to move 5 millimetres to the east

new-sci.title: A quantum state that lasts forever may finally be within our grasp
new-sci.description: Defying the laws of thermodynamics, experiments are beginning to show that a quantum state that is frozen forever might not be impossible. If we can tame it, it could unlock whole new types of matter

new-sci.title: Carl Sagan's The Demon-Haunted World is still supremely relevant today

new-sci.description: As the sun expands over the coming billions of years, Earth will become inhospitable to any life more complex than a microbe – but that might take longer than we thought

new-sci.title: New Scientist recommends an excellent look at the future of work

new-sci.description: Archaeologists have discovered traces of a wooden structure built 5000 years ago, 5 kilometres from Stonehenge, which appears to have been an even older monument for marking the summer solstice

new-sci.title: Cervical cancer deaths have plummeted thanks to HPV vaccine
new-sci.description: We already know the vaccine against human papillomavirus, or HPV, greatly reduces infections and cases of cervical cancer, and now we have the first evidence it prevents deaths too

new-sci.title: Chilling the body with drugs could limit brain damage from stroke
new-sci.description: Putting brain cells into a hibernation-like state via drugs that cool down core body temperature may help to preserve them following a stroke

new-sci.title: Oldest known plague outbreak killed hunter-gatherer children
new-sci.description: DNA evidence shows that plague bacteria devastated a community in Siberia more than 5000 years ago, challenging the idea that there were no major disease outbreaks before the advent of farming and large settlements

new-sci.title: Pigeons lock their eyes in place when they are flying
new-sci.description: Bird-mounted headsets and backpacks have revealed the surprising things pigeons do with their eyes when on the wing

new-sci.title: Our brains have their first thoughts surprisingly early in life
new-sci.description: By the time we’re born, our brains have all the hardware in place to form thoughts, and possibly even some conscious awareness

new-sci.title: Autism and ADHD are on the rise due to widening diagnostic criteria
new-sci.description: A study of 140,000 people suggests that a broadening of the diagnostic criteria for autism and ADHD explains the sharp rise in diagnoses, but that doesn't mean too many people are being told they are autistic or have ADHD

new-sci.title: Autism may have two distinct subtypes that vary by brain activity
new-sci.description: Evidence is mounting that there are distinct subtypes of autism, and now, scientists have found that the condition can vary according to the strength of people's brain connections

new-sci.title: The secrets to keeping your brain sharp in old age
new-sci.description: Neuroscientist Emily Rogalski studies superagers – people in their 80s or 90s with unusually keen memories, whose lifestyles suggest ways to slow cognitive decline

new-sci.title: Walking shark found in Papua New Guinea is new to science
new-sci.description: Hemiscyllium dudgeonae is the tenth recorded species of walking shark, which use their pectoral fins to move across reef flats, and its limited range means it may be at high risk of extinction

new-sci.title: Sperm have been made magnetic to allow IVF inside the body
new-sci.description: IVF could be done inside the body using a revolutionary technique that reduces the invasiveness of the traditional fertility treatment

new-sci.title: Arctic Ocean reaches tipping point that could be dire for marine life
new-sci.description: Disappearing sea ice is letting more sunlight in the Arctic Ocean and boosting phytoplankton growth, but this has depleted a crucial nutrient, which could severely affect animals higher up the food chain

phys-org.title: Laser pulses set layered metals vibrating 1 trillion times per second, revealing electron-driven motion
phys-org.description: How does light turn into motion within a metal? A team of researchers from European XFEL, the University of Potsdam and other participating institutions has shown that ultrashort optical laser pulses can trigger extremely rapid lattice vibrations in periodically layered metal structures—not primarily by heating the atomic lattice, but through the pressure exerted by hot electrons. The results are published in Nature Communications.

phys-org.title: Climate change is now causing more local extinction in temperate regions than the tropics, study shows
phys-org.description: Imagine returning to a favorite hiking trail 15 years after your first visit and discovering that many of the plants and animals that once lived there are gone. While these species may still exist elsewhere, these disappearances—known as local extinctions—are among the clearest signs that climate change is already transforming ecosystems and threatening species across the globe.

phys-org.title: Early warning tool may protect river fish in heat waves
phys-org.description: Researchers from the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research (WSL) have proposed a warning tool that predicts, up to three weeks in advance, when river fish in Switzerland will be at risk from heat. As heat waves become more frequent with climate change, this early warning system gives people time to act and protect fish populations from future heat waves.

phys-org.title: Low-development regions suffer far higher losses in climate disasters, study warns
phys-org.description: People living in regions with lower scores on the Human Development Index face a substantially higher risk from climate-related disasters, even when these are not unusually severe. This is the key finding of a new study led by researchers at Leipzig University. The study analyzed more than 7,000 climate-related disasters worldwide between 1990 and 2020 and combined these data with subnational indicators of human development. The work is published in the journal Nature Communications.

phys-org.title: Fermi mission uncovers possible sibling supernova remnants
phys-org.description: A new study of two supernova remnants, the debris left behind after stars explode, suggests the explosions came from stellar siblings that once orbited each other. The first star's detonation sent its binary companion hurtling through space, and then, after traveling for thousands of years, the surviving star blew up, too.

phys-org.title: Hidden fungus inside desert moss could rewrite 470-million-year story of how plants moved onto land
phys-org.description: Mosses are survivors. They can dry into what looks like green dust, only to spring back to life minutes after rain. They can grow on rocks, in deserts, and there's talk of using them to terraform Mars someday. According to new research, mosses have also been hiding something.

phys-org.title: How cracks in dry soil impact moisture evaporation
phys-org.description: Soils that are exposed to prolonged drought often develop desiccation cracks, which impact soil properties and exacerbate moisture loss through evapotranspiration. Now, a study from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign examines the evolution of soil cracking and how cracks interact with storage and movement of water in the soil. The findings can help improve hydrological models essential for water management. The research is published in the journal Soil and Tillage Research.

phys-org.title: How a telescope's mirror stability makes or breaks exoplanet detection
phys-org.description: Finding life beyond our solar system is a major goal of modern astronomy. NASA's planned Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) aims to take direct images of Earth-sized planets around stars other than our sun. This task, however, is extraordinarily difficult, given that these planets are roughly 10 billion times fainter than their host stars. To detect them, scientists must find ways to suppress nearly all of the nearby starlight, which would otherwise overwhelm the faint planetary signal.

phys-org.title: Trace additive unlocks faster bioplastic biodegradation without losing transparency or strength
phys-org.description: Compostable plastics could be part of a solution to the world's plastic waste problem. But currently these materials need industrial composting facilities to break down. In a step toward making a home-compostable plastic, researchers reporting in ACS Central Science have augmented polylactide (PLA)—a widely used biobased and compostable polymer—with a small amount of an additive. Tests show it helps the material degrade substantially faster without sacrificing critical qualities like streng

phys-org.title: Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer reveals four cosmic ray classes across 20 elements, defying current models
phys-org.description: Millions of light-years away, millions of years ago, a star exploded. In this violent process, it ejected incredible amounts of mass, including carbon, nitrogen and oxygen—the building blocks of life. In fact, the star may have produced elements on the periodic table all the way up to iron. As it exploded, it spewed these elements into deep space. Only a burnt-out core remained.

phys-org.title: Hubble glimpses merging galaxy clusters
phys-org.description: This NASA Hubble Space Telescope image features a galaxy cluster called CL0016+1609, or MACS J0018.5+1626, that is very bright at X-ray wavelengths and is one of the most extensively studied clusters at X-ray and radio wavelengths. X-ray observations of this cluster revealed that it is two clusters merging along our line of sight.

phys-org.title: Heat waves increase wildfire risk—a new study explains how much, and it's not a small number
phys-org.description: When heat waves hit the Western United States, the risk of wildfires quickly rises. The prolonged heat dries out vegetation, but that's only part of the cause—heat waves also play other roles in spreading wildfires.

phys-org.title: Greenland sees wildfires earlier in the year
phys-org.description: Greenland has recently been hit by localized wildfires, a rarity at this time of year that could be explained by global warming, a researcher at the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources said Thursday.

phys-org.title: Mating reveals cholesterol's hidden role in male fruit fly lifespan
phys-org.description: Scientists have discovered that the optimal diet for male fruit flies may depend strongly on whether they are reproducing, challenging long-standing assumptions about nutrition and aging. Led by researchers from the University of Liverpool's Department of Evolution, Ecology and Behavior, the international team used fruit flies to investigate how diet and reproductive activity influence lifespan and fertility.

phys-org.title: Five new springtail species discovered in China
phys-org.description: There is a Chinese saying that east or west, Guilin scenery is the best. Guilin and Chongqing, located in western China, are famous for their many mountains and rivers. They also harbor unique flora and fauna, such as the scaly-sided merganser, a globally endangered species restricted to eastern Asia.

phys-org.title: Missing DNA replication step revealed in first image of pre-initiation complex
phys-org.description: Cells have evolved careful checks to ensure DNA is copied only once, but how they switch on replication at the right moment has been the focus of a 30-year research question. New work from the Crick has recorded the missing step.

phys-org.title: Bedding structure controls rainfall runoff in mountain catchments
phys-org.description: Researchers at the University of Tsukuba have discovered that rainwater runoff in the highly rugged sedimentary rock mountains of Japan's Southern Alps is governed by two processes: "deep infiltration" and "shallow drainage via landslides." These processes are dictated by the inclination of geological strata. Based on these findings, the researchers propose a conceptual framework, termed the "structural ground system," to explain how the bedding structure regulates rainwater runoff.

phys-org.title: Ultrasound propagation in porous rocks: Theory identifies three distinct wave modes
phys-org.description: Ultrasound-based irradiation of rock formations has attracted considerable attention as a technique for enhancing heavy-oil (high-viscosity crude oil) recovery from deep underground reservoirs. However, a unified theoretical framework for wave propagation and energy dissipation in these formations remains lacking because water coexists with heavy oil within rock pores, and gas bubbles in the water respond dynamically to ultrasonic excitation, thereby creating a complex system.

undark.title: Making Sense of Data From Wearable Health Trackers
undark.description: Wearable health devices such as smartwatches, glucose monitors, and sleep trackers are blurring the line between consumer wellness and clinical medicine. One physician argues that validation standards and privacy protections must be established to ensure the usefulness of the data these devices generate.

undark.title: In California, a Plan to Help Wildlife Cross a Busy Freeway
undark.description: The 101 freeway in California bisects a mountainous region where threatened cougars and other animals are blocked without a viable path across 10 lanes of heavily trafficked roadway. But an ambitious 210-foot “vegetated bridge” will soon be home to what organizers say is the largest wildlife crossing anywhere in the world.

undark.title: Promising ‘Liquid Biopsies’ May Not Be Ready for Primetime
undark.description: Multi-cancer early detection tests seek to spot cancer from a single blood draw. Enabling earlier cancer diagnoses could help save lives and limit the need for invasive interventions. But while the tests are promising, physicians have expressed doubt about routine use by low-risk and asymptomatic individuals.

undark.title: Book Review: How Radio Astronomy Made the Invisible Visible
undark.description: According to astronomer Emma Chapman’s revelatory “The Echoing Universe,” the history of radio astronomy is filled with surprises that have revealed parts of the universe that would otherwise remain hidden and invisible — DIY instruments, secrets accidentally uncovered, and persistent connections to Earth.

undark.title: Risk Aversion in Science Stifles Innovation
undark.description: Does the scientific enterprise play it too safe? C. Brandon Ogbunu argues that risk-taking in science involves a willingness to reflect on the processes and incentives of the profession — and to dramatically overhaul them if they do not work. Only then can true scientific innovation take shape.

undark.title: A Peptide, a Secretive Scientist, and a Debate Over Evidence
undark.description: Access to unapproved peptides like BPC-157 has become a cause célèbre for the MAHA movement. Undark contributing editor Sara Talpos digs into the untold history of BPC-157 and its long journey from the scientific margins to the center of a debate over U.S. drug regulation.

undark.title: Book Review: Within Our Cells, the Miracle of Constant Mutation
undark.description: Our cells are constantly mutating in a battle for the survival of the fittest that is raging inside us daily, Roxanne Khamsi writes in “Beyond Inheritance.” Many of these mutations are harmless, others are cellular deviants that lead to disease, and remarkably, some can actually self-correct.

undark.title: The Six-Week Postpartum Checkup Comes Too Late
undark.description: In the U.S., maternity care generally ends with a checkup scheduled six weeks after giving birth. This single doctor’s appointment may be efficient for billing and discharge protocols, but the timing reflects the structure of the health care system more than the reality of maternal recovery.

undark.title: Book Review:  The Case for Making Data-Driven Decisions
undark.description: In “Beyond Belief: How Evidence Shows What Really Works,” science journalist Helen Pearson profiles a group of people working in medicine and other fields who became leaders of the worldwide evidence movement, which encourages the use of data from rigorous research to direct treatments, policies, and plans.

undark.title: What the Hantavirus Story Reveals About Medical Mistrust
undark.description: The reaction to an outbreak of hantavirus on a cruise ship reveals a story about mistrust in medicine and public health. In the U.S., hantavirus disproportionately kills Native Americans. A doctor who works at a hospital on Navajo Nation writes that such mistrust always lands hardest on the most vulnerable.

proj-syn.title: The Meaning of Limited Government—Then and Now
proj-syn.description: In 1776, Adam Smith and America’s founders envisioned an economy that allowed individuals to pursue their own material well-being, with minimal government intervention. Today, America’s Republican Party claims to be committed to restoring that laissez-faire ideal, even as they make a mockery of its animating principles.

proj-syn.title: AI Sovereignty Is About Options, Not Ownership
proj-syn.description: The US government’s abrupt decision to suspend foreign access to Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models clarifies what “AI sovereignty” is really about. In the emerging AI economy, competitive advantage will come not from owning a single model, but from being able to evaluate, select, and orchestrate many models.

proj-syn.title: The Promise and Peril of AGI
proj-syn.description: Artificial general intelligence could dramatically increase human prosperity and free people from countless mundane tasks. But unless its benefits and ownership are broadly shared, it could deprive billions of workers of their livelihoods and pave the way for a new form of techno-authoritarianism.

proj-syn.title: Reversing Brexit Is Labour’s Best Hope
proj-syn.description: When it comes to the relationship between the United Kingdom and the European Union, political expediency and economic logic both point in the same direction. A majority of British voters now believe that Brexit was a mistake, and they are looking for a leader who will put the issue back on the national agenda.

proj-syn.title: Global Health Reform Must Bolster Innovation
proj-syn.description: As funding falls for global public health, calls for a country-led system have grown louder. Such reforms are necessary, but they must not come at the expense of new vaccines, medicines, and diagnostics, which can be delivered by strengthening mechanisms—such as product development partnerships—that already work.

proj-syn.title: Learning from the Right Sovereign Wealth Funds
proj-syn.description: The Gulf has made establishing a sovereign wealth fund seem like a strategic—and glamorous—choice, leading countries like Canada to launch their own. But Latin America has run this experiment many times over the years, offering a more realistic view of an SWF’s pitfalls and promise.

proj-syn.title: Europe Cannot Afford Another Lost Year
proj-syn.description: European businesses need simpler rules, faster permitting, affordable energy, stronger infrastructure, and a fully functioning single market. The longer that European policymakers fail to deliver on these policies, the greater Europe’s competitiveness challenge will become.

proj-syn.title: White House Fight Night
proj-syn.description: The venue on the South Lawn for UFC Freedom 250 was built, approved, lit, filmed, defended, watched, and enjoyed as part of a celebration of freedom. President Donald Trump’s chosen object to represent that celebration was a cage.

proj-syn.title: The US-Iran Agreement Is a First Step
proj-syn.description: While the recently announced US-Iranian memorandum of understanding is certainly good news, it is not definitive. The path from a statement of diplomatic intent to a fully restored, non-inflationary energy supply chain is fraught with political, technical, and physical risks.

proj-syn.title: Developing-Country Risk Is Being Mispriced
proj-syn.description: When investors say there are no “bankable” projects in developing economies, they are typically referring less to project quality than to the cost of capital. But the assumptions driving up risk premia are not supported by the evidence, and until this changes, the misallocation of capital will continue to undermine development.

proj-syn.title: The Fed Has Been Honest and Stupid
proj-syn.description: It would be easy—and a mistake—to blame the US Federal Reserve’s many blunders on corrupt bureaucrats or imagined conspiracies. The truth of the matter is that the central bank relies on an outdated regional map and lagging indicators that no longer tell the whole story, while battling macroeconomic blazes that politicians stoke.

proj-syn.title: A New Framework for Climate Displacement
proj-syn.description: Global warming is already uprooting communities and impoverishing people who remain in vulnerable areas—a crisis that is often overshadowed by the focus on decarbonization. But the Global Climate Mobility Principles offer policymakers a framework for ensuring that these individuals maintain their agency and rights.

proj-syn.title: Peace With Iran Is All About Lebanon Now
proj-syn.description: US President Donald Trump says that he "calls the shots" on negotiating with Iran, and Israel has no choice but to submit to a deal that undermines its security interests. But a deal that makes Trump the protector of Lebanon—and, by extension, Iran-backed Hezbollah—could put the US and Israel on a collision course.

proj-syn.title: Every British Prime Minister’s Nightmare
proj-syn.description: The true nature of Britain’s “special relationship” with the United States has far more to do with American financiers’ willingness to keep borrowing to purchase British government debt than with history, culture, or Britain’s defense needs. Every UK Prime Minister must bear this burden, which is rapidly becoming unsustainable.

proj-syn.title: India’s Unfinished Reform Agenda
proj-syn.description: Elevated oil prices, potentially strong El Niño conditions during the monsoon season, and the tariff-induced fragmentation of global trade are bearing down on the Indian economy and will likely be a drag on GDP growth. But these adverse conditions may be a blessing in disguise if they force India to complete its economic reform agenda.

proj-syn.title: The Middle East’s New Normal
proj-syn.description: The most likely outcome of the Iran war is not peace but an unsatisfying ceasefire that leaves the underlying issues unresolved. This will mean an uneasy equilibrium in which Gulf countries go their own way, US influence wanes, and the regional order remains unsettled.

proj-syn.title: No Bridge Over Healing Waters for the G7
proj-syn.description: The French G7 presidency’s focus on global imbalances is both welcome and problematic. While long-standing trade imbalances between the United States, Europe, and China are, if anything, becoming even more troublesome, the leaders’ summit in Évian-les-Bains will do nothing to address the problem.

proj-syn.title: Are Government Stakes the Key to AI Sovereignty?
proj-syn.description: At first glance, reports that the US and Chinese governments are both considering taking stakes in national AI champions would seem to suggest a convergence between the world’s two leading AI powers. But a closer look reveals stark differences in their underlying strategies.
